content.overview: Section 17 provides that “fraud” means and includes any of the following acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party thereto or his agent, or to induce him to enter into the contract: (1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact; (3) a promise made without any intention of performing it; (4) any other act fitted to deceive; (5) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent. Mere silence as to facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances are such that regard being had to them it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech.
content.glance: Fraud = intentional deception by false suggestion, active concealment, hollow promise, act fitted to deceive, or legally declared fraud; mere silence not fraud unless duty to speak.
content.study: Fraud requires an act by a party (or with connivance or by agent) with intent to deceive or induce entry into the contract. The five limbs cover false suggestion of fact, active concealment, promise without intention to perform, any act fitted to deceive, and acts the law declares fraudulent. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech. Consent caused by fraud is not free (s. 14); the agreement is voidable under s. 19. Current-law framing: identify the act; prove intent to deceive or induce; exclude mere silence unless duty/speech; conclude voidability.

sections.heading: Five limbs of fraud
sections.body: False suggestion of fact; active concealment; promise without intention to perform; act fitted to deceive; act/omission law declares fraudulent.

sections.heading: Intent
sections.body: Committed by a party, or with connivance, or by agent, with intent to deceive or to induce entry into the contract.

sections.heading: Mere silence
sections.body: Mere silence is not fraud unless duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech.

examples.title: False suggestion of fact
examples.body: A asserts as fact something A does not believe to be true, intending to induce B to contract. That is fraud under s. 17(1).

hypotheticals.question: Is silence about a material fact always fraud?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 17 Explanation: mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech.

distinctions.title: Fraud (s. 17) vs misrepresentation (s. 18)
distinctions.right: May be without intent to deceive (unwarranted assertion believed true)

rows.right: Innocent or negligent positive assertion / breach of duty / causing mistake

misconceptions.correction: Fraud requires intent to deceive or induce, and fits one of the five limbs; misrepresentation is separate under s. 18.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 17 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the act (five limbs). II. Prove intent to deceive or induce. III. Apply silence rule. IV. Conclude voidability under s. 19.
